items.title: ‘Natural Realm Responded’: Filmmakers Detail Spiritual Manifestation on Set of New Movie
items.author: Tré Goins-Phillips
items.summary: Wow.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

In Romans, the Apostle Paul wrote about the earth pointing to God’s “eternal power and divine nature.” The Koomans, two filmmaking brothers, certainly sensed that while making their newest movie, “Daniel and the Fiery Furnace.”

It unfolded when Mena Massoud, portraying Daniel, and Elijah Alexander, playing King Nebuchadnezzar, filmed a scene on-location in India from Daniel 2, when the king — furious over astrologers who couldn’t interpret his dream — ordered Daniel’s execution. Facing his would-be killers, Daniel visited Nebuchadnezzar, asking for more time to petition God for an answer to the king’s dream “so they would not be executed along with the other wise men of Babylon” (Daniel 2:18, NLT).

When Massoud began reciting his lines, telling Nebuchadnezzar the meaning of his dream, Daniel and Matthew Kooman told CBN’s “Faith in Culture” the atmosphere on set shifted powerfully.

The scene centered on the latter part of Daniel 2, when Daniel foreshadowed the coming of Christ and what many biblical scholars believe to be a reference to Jesus’ triumphant return in the end times:

During the reigns of those kings, the God of heaven will set up a kingdom that will never be destroyed or conquered. It will crush all these kingdoms into nothingness, and it will stand forever. That is the meaning of the rock cut from the mountain, though not by human hands, and crushed to pieces the statue of iron, bronze, clay, silver, and gold. The great God was showing the king what will happen in the future. The dream is true and its meaning is certain” (Daniel 2:44-45, NLT).

“[Massoud is] speaking these words from Scripture, and a wind blows across the set,” Daniel Kooman recalled. “Behind the camera, tents were hitting walls and blowing off set. A rainstorm, a crack of thunder — things that we hadn’t experienced in the natural realm on any day leading up to that for 25 days of prep and shooting. None of these sort of occurrences were happening until those words of Scripture about the everlasting kingdom that is coming [were spoken].”

“All of a sudden,” he said, “the natural realm responded to those words of prophetic Scripture.”

With an impressive $1.2 million raised in crowdfunding, the Koomans said they are confident audiences are eager for epic-style theatrical films like “Daniel and the Fiery Furnace.”

More importantly, Matthew Kooman told CBN News he is confident the project has divine backing.

“God was clearly behind it from the beginning,” he said. “And we were blown away by just the success of raising funds through people who wanted to be a part of telling the biblical story. That’s what the real synergy was.”

Trusting in the Lord — and standing by the courage of one’s convictions — is critical to success in Hollywood, the brothers said, particularly for filmmakers making content retelling biblical stories.

Calling the project “incredibly challenging,” Daniel Kooman said the one thing that kept him and his brother grounded was constant meditation on the source material, the Old Testament book of Daniel, and a genuine belief in the inerrancy of the totality of Scripture.

The movie pulls cross references from all throughout the Bible. In addition to Daniel, the film blends in scriptural accounts from the the books of Psalms, Isaiah, Habakkuk, and Jeremiah.

“We found practically … we couldn’t take one step on any given day without a leading or a direction from the Lord,” said Daniel Kooman. “That can sound abstract, but, for us, it was like, ‘OK, what are we gonna do today and how is it going to have an impact?’ It’s only gonna be if it honors the Word.”

Pointing to Isaiah 55:11, which says Scripture “always produces fruit” (NLT), Daniel Kooman said he noticed a one-to-one correlation that, when they dedicated themselves to accurately retelling the story of Daniel as it’s depicted in the Bible, “there was an incredible blessing.”

“People on set — actors and people involved in the production — experienced that,” he said. “It was a daily occurrence of God’s help through the production.”

items.title: MTV Star Leaves Gay Lifestyle After Encounter With Jesus
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: Inspiring.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Davis Mallory was once an MTV star who lived an openly gay lifestyle while simultaneously adhering to what he called a Christian identity. 

Last year, though, “The Real World” star shocked fans when he shared a testimony during a Christian conference and it went viral. Then, earlier this month, he again found himself in the headlines after sharing images with his now-girlfriend. 

The initial reaction to his testimony was so intense last year that he said he faced death threats online in the wake of conservative and Christian activist Charlie Kirk’s murder.

This sparked a fair amount of fear in the reality TV star and singer — until God spoke through people and everything changed.

“I was singing in Hawaii and, on my flight home from Hawaii, I fell asleep on the plane, and I woke up, and all I heard was, ‘Lean not on your own understanding,’” Mallory said. “And I knew a little bit — that that was somewhere in the Bible, but didn’t know fully where it was. But I knew that God was saying, like, ‘I got you. You don’t understand what’s happening right now, Davis, but I got you.’” 

The next day, he had a dream where he was working with men in an Army bunker and he felt like God wanted him to be around other men of God. So, that night he went to a Bible study where he was prayed over. That same evening, a woman randomly approached him and said the Holy Spirit had prompted her to share a verse with him about fear. 

“She said, ‘I can tell you’re very afraid right now, and the devil wants you to stay afraid because you’ll make mistakes because you’ll trip,’” he recalled, noting that these events teamed with other messages from God finally brought him to a place of peace surrounding his story. 

This experience last year — and God’s provision — has enabled Mallory to speak out over the past few weeks and boldly share his journey to Jesus with total confidence.

“I have complete peace,” he said. 

The journey for Mallory has been a fascinating one, as his ascent on reality TV in many ways hinged on his formerly gay identity; today, it rests on Christ. 

“I … was thinking about the experience of being on a television show 200-plus years ago, making me famous for being gay, so to speak,” he said. “And the fact that I’m dating a girl today. If all of this was not on television, no one would know about it.“

Mallory, who grew up in a conservative and Christian household before initially coming out as gay, said there are many people going through similar circumstances in their personal lives, explaining that he believes God has used his journey and story to reach others. 

His journey is one that he’s openly reflecting on, explaining that he dated girls during his childhood before finding his affections turned toward men. Somehow, he said, being gay “overrid” his beliefs. But, over time, Mallory said everything transformed.

“For me, it was just gradual,” he said of his realization that homosexuality isn’t in line with God’s will. “It was failed relationship after failed relationship. It was falling in love with a man for him to then cheat on me with another man, and then to do it all over again, and all over again, and finding these relationships that were non-monogamous that were really lustful, and were really unfulfilling.”

Eventually, this mourning turned into questions. And when a Christian woman named Rachel came into Mallory’s life, he started digging deeper into faith — and questioning it all. When he attended a Christian conference and heard ex-porn star-turned-pastor Joshua Broome speak, something shifted.

“The fruits of my lifestyle was what was robbing me and it was actually Josh Broome and going to a Christian conference, hearing John 10:10 spoken where the devil comes to rob from you, to steal from you, and to kill you, and I thought about the homosexual lifestyle.” 

Mallory said he realized that the lifestyle was robbing peace from many around him, noting he had friends who had committed suicide and were unhappy; some even caught HIV. Others were simply unhappy that their expectations weren’t being met or found in same-sex relationships.

“I was just seeing that that lifestyle was really not producing the fruit of joy,” he said.

As Mallory’s friendship with Rachel grew, so did her spiritual influence. Over time, he started feeling an attraction to her and the two began dating — something that has transformed the MTV star’s life.

His relationship with Rachel has shown him a great deal about the true meaning of love.

“I was also seeing how lust will keep all of us attracted to every single person who’s beautiful because lust is just an attraction to beauty,” Mallory said. “But love is meeting the person that God designed for you.”

He continued, “And that was what I was finally feeling was this beautiful feeling of love, and I believe that every man, woman who has any kind of same-sex attraction can find this if they’re obedient and looking for it.”

Watch the rest of Mallory’s story above.

items.title: Andrew Garfield Is Still Searching
items.author: Emily Brown
items.summary: About five minutes into his conversation with RELEVANT, Andrew Garfield realizes some important context. He’s on a press day for The Uprising, Paul Greengrass’s new film about the Peasants’ Revolt of 1381, in which Garfield plays a farmer swept into the rebellion. The conversation has turned to John
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

About five minutes into his conversation with RELEVANT, Andrew Garfield realizes some important context.

He’s on a press day for The Uprising, Paul Greengrass’s new film about the Peasants’ Revolt of 1381, in which Garfield plays a farmer swept into the rebellion. The conversation has turned to John Ball, the radical priest played by Jamie Bell who helped inspire the real-life uprising, and whether faith and activism belong together.

Then it’s mentioned, almost in passing, that RELEVANT covers the intersection of faith and culture. Realizing that’s our lane doesn’t make Garfield more careful. He gets more specific.

He reaches for the priest on the docks in On the Waterfront. Then the Jesuits who marched against the Vietnam War and fought for civil rights. Eventually, he stops hedging.

“I think that spirituality, its rightful place, is within social justice,” he says. “I think that’s the best and most holy place for it. If you’re following the true teachings of Jesus, you’re not hanging out in the opulent gold ballrooms of the president. You’re hanging out with the people that need a miracle.”

It’s an unusually unguarded answer for a press day, but not an especially surprising one from Garfield. For the past decade, some of his most memorable roles have put faith under extraordinary pressure. He played a Jesuit watching his certainty collapse in Silence and a Christian medic refusing to carry a rifle in Hacksaw Ridge. In Under the Banner of Heaven, he was a Mormon detective slowly coming apart inside a murder investigation tangled up in religious fundamentalism.

Again and again, Garfield has ended up playing men trying to figure out what belief requires of them.

The Uprising is the most overtly political version yet. Somehow, Garfield also found it comforting.

The real revolt began over a deeply unpopular poll tax and spread through southeastern England, eventually sending thousands of rebels toward London. Despite the name history gave it, the Peasants’ Revolt wasn’t made up entirely of peasants. Tradespeople, townspeople and former soldiers joined the uprising too.

Greengrass brings the handheld, documentary-like style of Bloody Sunday, United 93 and Captain Phillips to that world, trading modern war zones for mud, farm tools and medieval England.

By the time Ploughman appears, he has already buried his family after the plague. He barely speaks. Then a poll-tax collector threatens someone in his community, and a man with very little left to lose gets pulled into the rebellion.

The film also plays with a much more familiar English legend. Shortly before release, Focus Features briefly retitled it The Uprising: The Rise of Robin Hood before dropping the subtitle. Robin Hood isn’t exactly a character in Greengrass’s version so much as an idea beginning to take shape.

“There’s this kind of hint at this archetypal green man, this Robin Hood archetype in our film,” Garfield says. “It’s a kind of emerging energy. It’s very indigenous to England. It’s a folk story.”

To Garfield, the appeal is less the outlaw himself than what he represents: a fantasy of justice emerging when the existing system has stopped working for ordinary people. But that isn’t ultimately what drew him to the script.

“It felt like a soul cry of a story,” he says. “A humanistic tale of longing — for connection to life, to meaning, to purpose, to dignity.”

“It’s a kind of survival story. But even more than that, it’s about what it is to have a soul, and about what it is to be a human being.”

The story may be more than six centuries old, but Garfield doesn’t talk about it like a history lesson.

“We all have a sense in the culture right now that there’s a lot that we’re missing the mark on,” he says. “There’s a lostness. It’s very easy to get lost.”

To Garfield, the film carries “a longing to get back on the right track, get back on the right path — as a species, really.”

The religious dimension of the revolt isn’t something Greengrass invented for the movie.

By 1381, John Ball had spent years antagonizing Church authorities with his preaching. In 1366, people were formally forbidden from attending his sermons. Historical accounts also describe him as excommunicated and repeatedly imprisoned, yet he continued preaching a radical message about social equality.

When the uprising began, rebels freed him from prison in Maidstone and brought him with them toward London.

At Blackheath, hostile chroniclers later attributed to Ball a sermon built around a line that outlived the revolt itself: “When Adam delved and Eve span, who was then the gentleman?”

The wording is disputed, but the point is hard to miss. If everyone descended from the same human family, what divine logic made one class of people masters of another?

Within days, rebels had entered London. After the revolt collapsed, Ball was captured and executed at St. Albans.

Garfield is less interested in treating Ball as a hero than in the ambiguity Bell brings to him.

“You can question what’s driving him, and when,” Garfield says. “Is it a spiritual quest that is for the greater good, or is it a more personal vengeance that is maybe more egocentric? I think that is the question and the line that our story is walking for all of these characters.”

The same uncertainty hangs over Ploughman. Garfield’s character wants justice, but the film keeps asking what happens when the pursuit of it becomes inseparable from rage.

Asked whether making The Uprising changed how he thinks about that tension, Garfield doesn’t manufacture an answer.

“I don’t have a good answer,” he says. “I don’t know if there is a definitive answer of certainty.”

Ploughman, he says, is “trying to find and walk that middle line,” looking for justice “through all of the ways that he knows how” while trying “to keep his faith within that pursuit.”

The middle gets harder to hold when one side has considerably more power than the other.

“At a certain point it’s possible that you realize that even though you’re acting in good faith, other people are not. The people with power are not,” Garfield says. “So then what do you do? You either lay down and die, or you fight for the dignity of your own soul and the souls of your brothers and sisters around you.”

Garfield may be uncertain about what justice permits. He’s less uncertain about whether faith should have anything to do with it.

That conviction predates The Uprising.

When Garfield first appeared on RELEVANT’s cover in 2016, he was promoting Hacksaw Ridge and preparing for the release of Silence. Even then, he was thinking about the relationship between spiritual conviction and people willing to confront the world around them.

“It does seem like the great figures, the great activists, the great men and women in history had a spiritual component to their lives that enabled them to do these superhuman things,” he said at the time.

A decade later, the instinct hasn’t changed much. The language has gotten sharper.

Garfield wasn’t raised in a religious home. Asked about his own faith in 2016, he described it as “free to roam.”

What he described was less a creed than an appetite. Growing up without religious belief, Garfield said, left him with the sense that something was missing.

“There was always something lacking,” he said.

Eventually, he began thinking about what people put in that empty space.

“As we know, if we don’t worship something healthy we’ll end up worshipping, more often than not, something rather unhealthy,” Garfield told RELEVANT. “Look at our consumer culture. Look at our celebrity culture. You name it. We worship the wrong thing — or if not the wrong thing, something that doesn’t actually feed us in a deep way.”

Preparing for Silence, Garfield spent a year studying Catholicism with Jesuit priest Father James Martin and undertaking the Spiritual Exercises of St. Ignatius. He also immersed himself in the work of Thomas Merton, the Trappist monk whose writing about faith and uncertainty deeply resonated with him.

“I connected with him so much because he seems to be always on the knife edge between faith and doubt,” Garfield said. “He seems to understand that the opposite of doubt isn’t certainty — that living with doubt is just as much a part of living with faith as faith itself.”

Garfield has resisted turning any of that into a neat conversion story. Certainty, in fact, has never seemed to interest him much.

What fascinated him in 2016 was the wager involved in trying to live according to something that can’t be completely verified.

“I think there’s something exquisitely, painfully beautiful about this — the attempt to live in accordance with something greater than ourselves, some greater ideal,” he said.

In the years since, the search has become more personal.

Garfield’s mother, Lynn, died of pancreatic cancer in 2019. Two years later, while promoting tick, tick… BOOM!, he told Stephen Colbert that he hoped his grief would never disappear.

“It’s all the unexpressed love that I didn’t get to tell her,” he said. “And I told her every day.”

Around the same time, he told GQ that the loss had intensified something already present in his life.

“I find spiritual pursuit to be the only pursuit, really, for me.”

There’s an echo of that loss in The Uprising. Garfield is playing a man who has buried his entire family before the movie has even properly begun.

By now, he has played enough spiritually restless characters that a pattern has emerged. There’s Silence’s Jesuit and the conscientious objector of Hacksaw Ridge. He stepped into the televangelist world of The Eyes of Tammy Faye, then played a Mormon detective questioning everything in Under the Banner of Heaven. Now there’s Ploughman.

Asked whether he sees a through line, Garfield takes a while before settling on one word.

“Searchers,” he says.

“Men who search for some deep place. Truth, understanding, connection, meaning, purpose. There’s a kind of search happening through this work.”

The same instinct shapes what he wants to make in the first place.

“Anything that feels connected to the deeper parts of what it is to be a person is where I’m looking, and where I’m feeling most compelled,” he says. “Stories that feel healing, that feel cathartic, that feel like reminders of the things that matter.”

When Garfield appeared on RELEVANT’s cover again in 2021, the story ended by observing that he had gotten unusually comfortable living with mystery.

Five years later, he still isn’t offering many answers.

The object of the search has shifted. In 2016, Garfield was talking about Merton’s ability to hold faith and doubt together. In The Uprising, the pressure falls on justice: What happens when fighting for it begins to threaten the convictions that sent someone into the fight?

The film doesn’t resolve the problem for him.

Near the end of the conversation, Garfield is asked whether that’s part of what draws him to movies like this, stories willing to leave their questions open. He starts to agree, then catches himself.

“Honestly, I think right now, maybe because we’re in a time of such uncertainty in the world and such kind of mass anxiety and pressure and hysteria and confusion,” he says. “Like, the world has no center right now.”

At the moment, Garfield doesn’t particularly want more uncertainty from his television.

He watches Dave, the 1993 Ivan Reitman comedy. He likes the Wham! documentary. He puts on the Paddington movies.

“I wanna watch things that feel comforting,” he says.

Which makes The Uprising an unlikely candidate.

Ploughman loses almost everything. The rebellion turns bloody. Whatever justice its characters are reaching for arrives, if it arrives at all, in a form considerably smaller than victory.

And yet:

“Making The Uprising, reading The Uprising and watching The Uprising has felt very comforting to me,” Garfield says. “Because my body can relax. Because I’m like, yeah, this is true. There’s something that I’m watching in this story that resonates really deep.”

By the end, Ploughman has lost most of what once gave him a place in the world.

“He thinks he is lost entirely,” Garfield says. “But what he finds is a connection to the everything.”

Garfield seems to have found something in the film too. Not an answer, exactly. More like evidence that the questions bothering him aren’t his alone.

“There’s something — I’m not alone in this longing for change,” he says. “I’m not alone in this longing for change. And I think there’s something quite soothing about that. And invigorating as well.”

items.content:
📖 Podcast | Theology in the Raw

Today on the show, our host, Bri, answers a listener's question: "what grounds you after a mentally challenging day?". Bri shares her top self-care strategies and tips to help you wind down after a tough day, drawing from her own experiences and focusing on mindfulness practices, meditation, deep breathing exercises, and more relaxation techniques for stress relief. We can release the energy that does not serve us and we can feel great and empowered, as we deserve to. Mental wellness and emotional wellbeing are some of the pillars of WellBriing, and we're so excited for you to be inspired by this episode.

Extra bonus content: a special guided meditation inspired by this episode is available now, here on the WellBriing Podcast, titled "Guided Meditation: Relaxing and Letting Go to Feel Empowered". Visit our podcast feed to find it right next to this episode!

Please follow the podcast and connect with us on all social platforms @wellbriing! Connect with our host, Bri, on Instagram @bri.healthy.

Have a beautiful, amazing day! Thank you for being here and for being you!

items.title: Psychotherapy or Confession?
items.author: Dr. D.P. Curtin
items.summary:
Dr. D.P. Curtin

In the Catholic world, it is more apparent—and it needs to be stated—that therapy and confession are not the same enterprise.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Dr. D.P. Curtin

They say that everyone’s favorite subject is themselves. People are endlessly skilled in discussing themselves, their thoughts and feelings, their ideas for the way the world should be. Take any contemporary American and place them in a coffee shop, on a podcast, or in a therapist’s office, and they can produce a forty-five-minute dissertation on their childhood and all those assorted things that punctuate life. In the last quarter-century in particular, we have become connoisseurs of our own interiority. The language of psychology, once reserved for the consultation room, has puzzlingly entered into common usage. We know our attachment styles, our personality types, our love languages, our trauma responses, and perhaps even the unconscious motives that prevent us from finishing tasks. If self-knowledge alone could save us, ours would be the most pristine, most devout generation since the apostles walked in Galilee. However, perhaps self-knowledge alone is an incomplete discipline.

Something curious has happened in the wake of all this psychological banter. In short, the more fluent we have become in the language of psychological introspection—in the act of explaining ourselves—the less certain we seem about changing ourselves. This is by no means an indictment of psychotherapy or a claim against its efficaciousness. Good counseling has aided countless people from the personal trials of depression, addiction, anxiety, grief, and despair. It has given us the verbiage to rebuild communication and offered us recognition of our own need for boundaries and personal limitations. It would be foolish to deny the value of this in the face of overwhelming results.

However, there is some confusion relating to what psychotherapy is and what it can do. In the Catholic world, it is more apparent—and it needs to be stated—that therapy and confession are not the same enterprise. They are relatives, not twins. For the unfamiliar, there has been speculation that Freud got the idea for his “talking cure” in his own Viennese childhood. His Austrian Catholic nanny would often take him to church, and he would observe firsthand the affective changes that took place before and after the sacrament of auricular confession. Taking this account at face value, this would make confession something akin to psychotherapy’s great-grandfather. However, with this, as with most relations, there are considerably different qualities to both of these crafts. The first of which is an orientation to the subject. That is to say, psychotherapy ordinarily asks, What happened to you? while confession asks, What have you done? The difference here is not trivial, albeit subtle. One question seeks understanding. The other is seeking something alien to the realm of psychology: the idea of repentance.

Suffice it to say that modern people greatly prefer the first because it allows us to remain self‑preoccupied. Psychotherapy is built on the premise of constructivism, that you are the authority on your own life, happiness, and the pursuit of the good in the world. The second is considerably less flattering. It insists that after every generous allowance has been made for our upbringing, there still remains one stubborn fact: We are responsible for ourselves. We possess the free will capable of making the decisions that ultimately plague us. In the words of the late Edwin Arnold, “Ye suffer from yourselves, none else compels.”

To be frank, there is no market for that kind of observation. As a rule latent found across our civilization, human beings have always preferred complicated explanations to simple confessions. It is comforting and perhaps self-aggrandizing to imagine ourselves as elaborate machines requiring expert technical calibration. Every age invents new vocabularies for old vices, as though a change in terminology amounted to a change in human nature. It is rather less pleasant to admit the obvious fact that pride, vanity, and selfishness have survived through every century without requiring much in terms of innovation. The old hypocrites of yesteryear at least paid virtue the compliment of imitation.

The sacrament of confession is radical precisely because it refuses to let us be passive in our actions, to become spectators of our own moral lives. It does not permit the participant to be detached. It invites us to analyze our misgivings and personal failings from a safe academic distance. It requires us to stand inside the moral wreckage of our own actions and admit, without annotation or legal counsel, “I am the one accountable.” In the era that we live in, that sentence has become unambiguously countercultural. We are inhabitants of an age that is remarkably proficient at distributing blame—or rather finding absolution for ourselves and condemnation for others. Our vices are accompanied by a long personal genealogy of behavior. Every one of our failings has a context, and every one of our cruelties possesses a reasonable explanatory framework. While some of those explanations are in fact valid and deserve thoughtful consideration, explanation and absolution are very different things.

To explain why a bridge collapsed is not the same as rebuilding it. Likewise, understanding why we sin, why we have transgressed the natural moral order of the world, does not reconcile us with God or with our neighbor. It only provides the prologue, the route by which we brought ourselves there. The act of any confession begins where explanation ends.

The state of our culture has become emotionally allergic to any sense of judgment. For the lay person, the idea of judgment is akin to moral violence. Perversely, our culture has imagined freedom as the absence of any kind of judgment, and in doing so, has created a landscape of perpetual and inexhaustible nihilism. Christianity proposes something altogether stranger. Our freedom begins not with moral judgment but with truthful judgment. I help no one by condemning them, but I also cannot help them if I deny them the truth that they need. A person who cannot admit to their own sin, who is not responsible for themselves, is not liberated from sin but a slave to their own insanity.

The confessional performs a remarkable act, something which has little parallel in the course of Western civilization. It removes every respectable disguise we all carry. There is no room for temporal authority. There is no room for political opinion or professional accomplishments. In the end, there are no excuses. Inside, there is only the sinner asking for mercy. It is difficult to think of another institution in our civilization that so thoroughly levels any notion of human pride. The Church does not ask whether your failures were sophisticated or what unconscious forces drove you to act. It only asks whether they are yours and you repent of them.

If my deepest problem is only my environment, the society I live in, the friends or family that surround me, then I must wait for the whole rest of the world to improve before I can become better. Obviously, such a proposition is impossible, and it shifts accountability to everyone and anyone. If everything is determined by forces outside my control, then genuine moral transformation becomes exceedingly difficult to imagine. Christianity, with its proposition of sin, redemption, and renewal, proposes a harder diagnosis but a brighter hope.

Sin is real, but so is the presence of grace. The Christian leaves the confessional with something no amount of self-analysis can provide: not insight into the nebulous past but reconciliation for the future. Psychotherapy may help us understand why we fell and offer us the natural comfort of connecting with another human being. However, confession assures us that, by God’s grace, we need not remain on the ground. In an age devoted to explaining ourselves, that may be the most subversive idea of all.

items.title: WOF 544 | Modern Christian Martyrdom
items.author: Dr. Matthew Petrusek
items.summary:
Dr. Matthew Petrusek

In this new conversation, we’ll explore the specific witness of Christian martyrs, and examine this modern era of Christian persecution.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Dr. Matthew Petrusek

Welcome back to the Word on Fire Show. I’m Matthew Petrusek, senior director of the Word on Fire Institute and the host of the Word on Fire Show. Thank you for joining us. Recently, Dr. Tod Worner of The Evangelization & Culture Podcast sat down with Bishop Barron to discuss modern Christian persecution with Bishop Barron’s new book, What Do Their Deaths Demand? Now, it’s a topic we’ve explored here on this show, once before. In this new conversation, we’ll take a deeper dive into that subject, exploring the specific witness of some of these martyrs, and examining this modern era which has seen more Christian persecution than any other in history. Here to discuss that with Dr. Tod Worner, is Bishop Robert Barron.
